metadata.title: Claude, Salesforce API.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether an empty response from Salesforce's REST API means a write failed, using the salesforce-api skill's own documented facts as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that 204 with no body is success, and that a call bundling several writes needs each subrequest's own status checked, not just the outer one.

beats.narration_text: Someone PATCHes a Salesforce record, gets an empty response back, and assumes it broke. Here's what's actually happening — 204 No Content is what a clean write looks like. So how do you tell success from failure?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'An empty response from Salesforce means my update failed.', hesitates on 'failed', corrects to 'worked', lands the real question

beats.narration_text: PATCH a Salesforce record cleanly and the API answers with 204 and a completely empty body — that emptiness is the success signal. Get a field name wrong and the same call comes back with a real body this time: a JSON array, with an errorCode inside it. Salesforce optimized for silent success over uniform responses, so success stays quiet and failure always talks back — and never as a plain object. This works if you're checking the status code; it fails if you were expecting one consistent shape.

shot.new_visual_element: A clean PATCH returns 204/empty; a bad-field PATCH returns a JSON array with an errorCode — same call shape, opposite bodies

production_viz.label: Silent success, loud failure
production_viz.mechanic: Two request cards submit side by side — CLEAN UPDATE and BAD FIELD NAME. Both PATCH the same record shape. The clean one resolves to an empty 204 card. The bad-field one resolves to a JSON-array card with an errorCode inside it, flagged terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Every call needs the org's own instance URL — its My Domain — plus the versioned data path. There's no shared endpoint across orgs; Salesforce optimized for tenant isolation at the cost of one clean base URL. Before touching a field, Describe the object: field names, picklist values, and which fields are actually updateable — the schema check the API won't do for you at write time. Then query the open Opportunities closing this quarter, with Account name and owner, and pull the Id of the top match — that's the record about to change.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — instance URL + Describe confirm StageName is updateable, then the SOQL query returns the top Opportunity's Id

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — instance URL, Describe, then query
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. An instance-URL tag locks in (org My Domain + versioned path). A Describe card confirms StageName: updateable=true, picklist includes Closed Won. Below, a SOQL query card 'open Opportunities · closing this quarter · Account name + owner' submits and returns a single Id stamp for the top match. THIS EXACT ID RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: PATCH that same Id's StageName to Closed Won, and the response comes back 204 — empty, and exactly what a successful update looks like. Chain several updates in one Composite call instead, and the outer 200 doesn't mean every subrequest succeeded. Each subrequest carries its own httpStatusCode, and only checking those individually tells you which wrote and which didn't. That's Composite's design — batching for throughput at the cost of one uniform success signal. And a failed subrequest doesn't undo the others either, unless allOrNone was set to true — otherwise the batch's partial writes stay put. This works if you value throughput; it fails if you needed atomicity.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same Id's PATCH resolves 204; then a Composite batch of several PATCHes, outer 200, each subrequest's own status checked individually

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — 204, then the Composite caveat
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 ID RETURNS, identical, PATCHed to Closed Won, resolving to an empty 204 card — exactly what success looks like. Below, a Composite batch of three PATCH subrequests submits under one outer 200. Each subrequest card carries its own httpStatusCode — two read 200/204, one reads 400, flagged terracotta. A small allOrNone toggle sits beside it: false, so the two good writes stick despite the one failure.

beats.narration_text: An empty response from Salesforce isn't a failure — 204 with no body is what success looks like. Trust the status code, not the silence. And when one call carries several writes at once, check each subrequest's own code, not just the outer one wrapping them.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — read it with me. Find all open Opportunities closing this quarter in my Salesforce org, with Account name and owner, then update the top one to Closed Won. Watch three things: does it set the org's real instance URL before making any call, does it Describe the Opportunity object to confirm StageName is updateable and Closed Won is a valid picklist value before writing, and does it check the actual status code afterward instead of treating an empty response as a failure. Go deeper: ask the same model why Salesforce made silent 204s the success signal for writes in the first place — what did that optimize for, and what did it cost the caller? Liam, in for Bear.
